content: I have been following the development of Tau Ceti attentively with the purpose of gleaning insights about how to make mathlib's human-powered processes more efficient. Today I would like to discuss one aspect of Tau Ceti that I believe mathlib could benefit greatly from copying: roadmaps.

I see four closely-related problems with the way mathlib is currently being grown:

  1. Contributors each have their own agenda which is not usually effectively communicated to reviewers.
  2. Conversely, reviewer's' attention is scattered at random (literally! by an algorithm!) across broad areas of maths (the t- labels).
  3. Newcomers lack direction in terms of what to contribute to mathlib, which is unsurprising since directions we want to push mathlib in aren't properly advertised, and often end up starting their own agenda instead of joining existing forces. In the worst cases, their agendas have no relevant maintainer, and we have to turn their contributions away.
  4. Many expert mathlib contributors have opinions about how such or such topic should be formalised or even prototypes or full formalisation, but these opinions/formalisations aren't recorded in a centralised manner/at all.

I believe these could all be addressed by roadmaps, by which I mean the following:

  1. Each roadmap would be a .md file in the mathlib repository documenting some mathematical results in the form of an item list, as well as design decisions to take into account when formalising, or pointers to formalisations outside of mathlib.
  2. Each roadmap would have a lead contributor, a lead maintainer and potentially more contributors, maintainers and reviewers assigned to it.
  3. Assigning a contributor/reviewer/maintainer to a roadmap requires their approval.
  4. Contributors would have to declare which roadmap any feat PR is part of, potentially with a label, and tick off the relevant items from it. If their PR doesn't is any existing roadmap, they would be invited to first contribute a new roadmap.
  5. Chore and refactor PRs too can be declared as part of a roadmap (like preliminary cleanups, bigger refactors), but don't have to. Authors of big refactors are encouraged to document them in the relevant roadmap(s).
  6. PRs belonging to a roadmap are assigned in priority to reviewers and maintainers of said roadmap.
  7. A single roadmap should equate the content of 10-100 PRs. For example it cover the material necessary to build up to a landmark result, or the content of one chapter of a textbook.
  8. Roadmaps can depend on each other in an acyclic fashion. Roadmaps that transitively depend on 4-5 or more roadmaps are frowned upon.

By design, roadmaps solve the problem of PRs being out of scope by not having reviewers: Since any feat PR needs to belong to a roadmap, the lack of reviewer/maintainer expertise/capacity will be spotted before the feat PR is even opened (and hopefully before the code is even written/cleaned up for mathlib). If a contributor is told that their potential contribution is out of scope, then hopefully they can divert their efforts to an existing roadmap instead, keeping mathlib's growth focused.

Conversely, reviewers/maintainers will be more focused in their reviewing and avoid having to become jacks
of all trades. This is also potentially an issue: if we compartimentalise mathlib reviewing to this extreme, we might end up with diverging opinions on how to design mathlib. Hopefully not to an extent that can't be fixed with a Zulip discussion/maintainer meeting.

Roadmaps as I am suggesting them are similar to t- , but are intentionally much narrower in scope, so that a reviewer/maintainer being assigned to a PR from a roadmap they are assigned to is almost guaranteed to be able to review the PR. IMO roadmaps could even fully replace the t- labels, my only apprehension being about refactors.

Roadmaps as I am suggesting them are also similar to github projects, but have a big advantage over them: changes can be reviewed. This means that we can let anyone contribute a change to a roadmap while ensuring that its content is still in scope for mathlib and its reviewing capacity.
Presumably “lead contributor” don’t necessarily have to be a maintainer/reviewer, but just anyone who writes a roadmap

I agree re the problem
One thought that comes to mind reading this solution is that this approach requires a higher level of commitment from contributors
Maybe that's fine - I suppose you're asking for people to take explicit responsibility for their "agendas"
But like, we're not being paid, so it's easy for people to just vanish, gumming up this more rigid system

I think it should be people that have at least some experience of contributing "feature" PRs to mathlib. In no big software project would you come up and be like "hey dear rust team, I am new and I will rewrite your parser or a new shiny feature". If you want to contribute to a high-profile project you have to start with smaller contributions. On the flip side I think there needs to be options of smaller projects that are available for interested newcomers; the problem that I see is that all of these small projects might be immediately gobbled up by people letting their LLM loose on them and it does not achieve the goal of training people.

Yaël Dillies said:

This is also potentially an issue: if we compartimentalise mathlib reviewing to this extreme, we might end up with diverging opinions on how to design mathlib.

I think having these diverging opinions stem from explicit design decisions in "roadmaps" would be a vast improvement on the status quo, where they only come up once a code conflict arises.

The flipside is that this way expects a higher level of commitment of lead contributors.

@Yaël Dillies if people like this idea, would you be willing to organise it informally, in advance of any possible requirement to use this system?
I would be keen to write up a roadmap and discuss my plans with others!

Moritz Doll said:

I think there needs to be options of smaller projects that are available for interested newcomers

Smaller parts of bigger projects, or smaller standalone projects? The goal of my proposal is to avoid the latter one, to focus attention on the big projects.

Artie Khovanov said:

Yaël Dillies if people like this idea, would you be willing to organise it informally, in advance of any possible requirement to use this system?
I would be keen to write up a roadmap and discuss my plans with others!

Yes of course! My whole idea stemmed from seeing the Tau Ceti roadmap on the representation theory of finite abelian groups and thinking "Wouldn't it be great if mathlib had a similarly focused effort to instead the representation theory of uniformly almost-periodic functions over any group following von Neumann?" (that would be the mathlib generality version of rep theory of finite abelian groups), so I would be willing to write such a roadmap once the design has become clear to me (I am maybe a month away from understanding the relevant literature)

Yaël Dillies said:

Moritz Doll said:

I think there needs to be options of smaller projects that are available for interested newcomers

Smaller parts of bigger projects, or smaller standalone projects? The goal of my proposal is to avoid the latter one, to focus attention on the big projects.

Yes, the former

One thing that could also be useful is to use the Tau Ceti roadmaps as roadmaps for mathlib as well. I know the scope and generality might not be quite there, but IMO one useful thing mathlib can gain from Tau Ceti is using it as a testing ground for what should be done in mathlib. For example you can see how Tau Ceti, defined, say, an adic space and then how its used in the code. You can then quickly see whats good/bad with those choices.

Chris Birkbeck said:

For example you can see how Tau Ceti, defined, say, an adic space and then how its used in the code.

I think this is in general a very bad idea unless you've already thought hard about it first. AIs and humans alike are quite susceptible to having that knowledge (of an existing approach) inhibit their ability to invent novel ones. I'm not saying it's impossible, to be clear, just significantly harder.
Oh interesting, I hadn't thought of it like this, the use case I had in mind is like what happened here: #42312
I like the proposal. Will there be a rule that to open a PR that works on a roadmap, you first need to discuss this with the lead contributor and get their approval?

An issue I see is that the good design can often not be guessed at the start of a project: it's only by implementing a design and playing with it that you can see its weaknesses and how it should be improved.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

I like the proposal. Will there be a rule that to open a PR that works on a roadmap, you first need to discuss this with the lead contributor and get their approval?

I'd lean against that level of ridigity
I'd rather say there should be a roadmap dashboard which the lead contributor will naturally be expected to monitor

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

An issue I see is that the good design can often not be guessed at the start of a project: it's only by implementing a design and playing with it that you can see its weaknesses and how it should be improved.

I don't think that is an argument against roadmaps. If you decide to change a design, then the corresponding roadmap can be updated to reflect this.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

An issue I see is that the good design can often not be guessed at the start of a project: it's only by implementing a design and playing with it that you can see its weaknesses and how it should be improved.

As I understand Yaël's proposal, it will make it easier to do this in a slightly decentralised way, because the roadmap can always be amended. Although this does indeed give the lead contributor quite some power over the design direction, I suspect this simply formalises existing implicit relationships - I've found myself commenting on others' PRs to say no this is the wrong way to do things.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

An issue I see is that the good design can often not be guessed at the start of a project: it's only by implementing a design and playing with it that you can see its weaknesses and how it should be improved.

This is what I have in mind when I say having Tau Ceti as a testing ground.
There is a big difference between "implementing a design and playing with it" and "letting some AI implement something and play with it"

One thing that might be interesting to consider is maintaining some / all of these 'roadmaps' as downstream projects instead of in mathlib4 itself. This way, development of a roadmap can become decentralized and move 'faster', but with established guidelines and a 'strict' goal of 'everything is meant to be upstreamed eventually'.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

Will there be a rule that to open a PR that works on a roadmap, you first need to discuss this with the lead contributor and get their approval?

It also solves this problem, because each of the repos can establish its own governance.

Historically this model has existed 'de facto': a lot of projects have ToMathlib folders that are meant for upstreaming, and we have some tooling to support this scenario. Making more explicit this notion of a 'blessed satellites to Mathlib' would allow us to establish standards around them and subsequently enable building a bunch tooling / infra support (caching, etc.) where appropriate.

Of course there would be some formal process to become one of these 'blessed' downstreams (the same way a roadmap should be approved initially), and this is how you achieve the 'centralization' that is lacking today. One can see the obvious translation of Yael's proposal here #mathlib4 > Roadmaps and the growth of mathlib @ 💬 to a roadmap living in another repo instead of as mathlib4 subfolders.

I can definitely find some drawbacks though:

  • The roadmaps could evolve without 'mathlib reviewer' supervision and diverge quickly to 'un-upstreamable'. This doesn't hurt mathlib4 as a library, but it would be an unfortunate 'waste of time'.
  • Losing the monorepo structure means that coordinating changes across roadmaps is hard. Here, standardized structure and automation could help

A single roadmap should equate the content of 10-100 PRs

Let me take a recent example, defining quotient manifolds. This was a group project I supervised at ItaLean (in Bologna, last December); to me this is a nice and relatively self-contained project that definitely belongs to mathlib. (It also worked nicely as a group project.)

Most of that work and its follow-ups have been merged by now; #40727 would be the seventh PR in that sequence. I can foresee at least one more PR (proving smoothness of the projection), and a ninth one about applying this to e.g. defining complex projective space as a smooth manifold. However, this could also have been 5 PRs.

We don't want to split PRs artificially to reach such a threshold, or urge roadmap writers to inflate theirs just to hit such a limit. I think we should have space for smaller roadmaps, if well-justified.

I think having roadmaps you can assign feat PRs to is a good thing, however I think forcing feat PRs to be part of roadmaps probably would lead to bad consequences.

Yaël Dillies said:

  1. Chore and refactor PRs too can be declared as part of a roadmap (like preliminary cleanups, bigger refactors), but don't have to. Authors of big refactors are encouraged to document them in the relevant roadmap(s).

I think this would have to include adding small lemmas (like to t-data), which one might see missing from i.e. downstream projects.

But more importantly I think very often it is nice to add concepts which are definitely not worth a roadmap, but still good to have.
For example, a while ago I added Carmichael numbers to mathlib in two PRs (#42801 and #43417). There is not too much to say beyond that about them that fits mathlib that I am aware of (except computational aspects which also wouldnt need more than a couple of PRs).
So Carmichael numbers most likely this would not fit to any specific roadmap (+ not be worth their own) and thus be lost. I think this happens quite often; I imagine many leaf files fit this pattern.

I am also worried this could intimitade well-meaning new-contributors. When I made my first PRs it was always a little bit scary (even though it was just small lemmas) and I dont think having to put a PR into an existing, serious roadmap (which I may not have fully understood the mathematics of) would have helped this.

I think the big benefit of roadmaps as proposed by Yaël is that they soft-commit the future direction of a part of Mathlib, encouraging discussion to happen at a higher level than PR by PR. A downstream project being upstreamed doesn't do that in the same way, and doesn't provide the same incentive to explain a design even as it evolves to the rest of the community.

So I think having the roadmap md files and some sort of ownership over them by experienced contributors is crucial to making anything like this work (whether or not it's mandatory)

Chris Birkbeck said:

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

An issue I see is that the good design can often not be guessed at the start of a project: it's only by implementing a design and playing with it that you can see its weaknesses and how it should be improved.

This is what I have in mind when I say having Tau Ceti as a testing ground.

AI can easily handle those nasty 20+line goals without feeling any pain. If a goal in the infoview is unreadable, I would go back and fix some API. I want to know if Tau Ceti tests such human sensible inconvenience.

Marcelo Lynch said:

One thing that might be interesting to consider is maintaining some / all of these 'roadmaps' as downstream projects instead of in mathlib4 itself. This way, development of a roadmap can become decentralized and move 'faster', but with established guidelines and a 'strict' goal of 'everything is meant to be upstreamed eventually'.

Although they could help for development, I see roadmaps more as a way to coordinate upstreaming of existing code. Maybe the optimal roadmap would be one where a third of the unticked items are proved in a downstream repo, at any point in time. This way there is evidence that this roadmap is already accessible, and there is also space for more contributors to join the development.

Michael Rothgang said:

A single roadmap should equate the content of 10-100 PRs

Let me take a recent example, defining quotient manifolds. This was a group project I supervised at ItaLean (in Bologna, last December); to me this is a nice and relatively self-contained project that definitely belongs to mathlib. (It also worked nicely as a group project.)

Most of that work and its follow-ups have been merged by now; #40727 would be the seventh PR in that sequence. I can foresee at least one more PR (proving smoothness of the projection), and a ninth one about applying this to e.g. defining complex projective space as a smooth manifold. However, this could also have been 5 PRs.

We don't want to split PRs artificially to reach such a threshold, or urge roadmap writers to inflate theirs just to hit such a limit. I think we should have space for smaller roadmaps, if well-justified.

I was careful to say "_the content of_ 10-100 PRs", not "10-100 PRs", by which I meant to point out that the content could reasonably be spread across that many PRs but doesn't actually have to be. For your specific example though, I think "The quotient of a manifold is a manifold" is too narrow of a roadmap, and instead we would have made "Standard manifold constructions" be the roadmap, or something like that.

Yaël Dillies said:

Although they could help for development, I see roadmaps more as a way to coordinate upstreaming of existing code. Maybe the optimal roadmap would be one where a third of the unticked items are proved in a downstream repo, at any point in time. This way there is evidence that this roadmap is already accessible, and there is also space for more contributors to join the development.

That makes sense. In general I am still interested in having some more 'canonical structure' (and tooling) for these 'dowstreams meant for upstreaming' (today this is basically 'the ForMathlib directory'). Maybe 'being part of a roadmap' can end up pushing us in this direction.

Although I agree with the need of more structure for downstream repos, I don't think roadmaps would do much to introduce such structure, except possibly for the fact that they would require such structure to e.g. record the declarations relevant to a roadmap and check that the declarations actually exist.

I'm all for TODOs/issues/projects/blueprints, but tbh this proposal makes me very worried.
It depends on what you mean exactly, but if I'm understanding the proposal correctly then none of my PRs are likely to be accepted if this goes through, and I think there are many others in the same boat.

You've mentioned that the plan includes closing PRs not in roadmaps. Even if you remove this rule, I think the existence of "roadmaps" (which aren't perceived as equivalent to projects) will lead to some maintainers enforcing this rule in practice regardless. I really think the solution is to encourage opening issues / projects / proof-wanteds / collaborations, and not make mathlib into Tau Ceti.

I'm also worried about this "lead contributor" thing, since it sounds like whoever creates the roadmap must also work towards it (or nominate such a person), like the project-intentions. So maintainers can't just suggest something they want to see contributed to mathlib.

Please don't. (unless of course I've misunderstood it completely)

Let me propose an experiment: Create a rough high-level draft of roadmaps that make sense to you, then keep them private for a month (but maybe publish their hashes) and count how many PRs in that month would have been closed under this new system.

This would measure how much you're affecting the status quo of Mathlib contributions, and perhaps how many contributors would be effectively banned because of this.

To avoid lots of work, I think each such roadmap draft could look like a table-of-contents from a book, so that it would be easy to make them alone. (and hopefully they'll be devoid of LLM fluff trying to hit a word quota)

Over the past year, the number of PRs on the queue at any one time has gone from ~300 to ~700, and the number maintainer merged from ~30 to ~70, even under increasing review capacity. I do think we need more structure if we want to increase the growth rate while maintaining quality.

I guess my point is that PRs are getting through slower and slower and so it's difficult to do any focused upstreaming or big refactors requiring multiple PRs, as opposed to more self-contained local clean-ups or API completion. We need to redistribute effort towards high-level planning.

Just a brief follow up since I expressed similar concerns as Snir and Felix in the earlier thread: I actually do think that having roadmaps could be a very positive thing. I just would leave a little wiggle room (both de jure and de facto) for work that doesn't fit in a roadmap shaped box (t-linter, t-meta, etc.) and still make it possible for well-meaning beginners that aren't just lobbing LLM-written code into a PR to learn how to contribute.

I think roadmaps would be great (some may remember that we used to have them, long ago! :-), but I would like to make sure we are very clear that they never prevent anything. No reviewer should ever be saying "no, the roadmap says to do it differently" (maybe at most they should be saying "I'll tell the roadmap author we've gone in a different direction", but shouldn't even be putting that as an expectation on a PR author).

I think roadmaps would in practice constrain a PR going in a different direction, and I don't think this is a bad thing. I think sometimes a discussion needs to be had at the level of the roadmap rather than the level of the PR, and that's OK! Of course this is very different to eg closing a PR because it doesn't comply with a roadmap.

If this is of any help, I can give the recent perspective of a (I believe) well-meaning beginner: when I started learning lean last year, I decided to engage with the PR review process because I thought it would be a good exercise and I would learn good practices / become useful. I was very motivated and spent hours trying to find an approach to this. It was extremely overwhelming, to see this endless sea of PRs, and not discern any structure. I think something like what you are suggesting here might have helped engage with the process.

I have a similar experience; relatedly I believe some well-meaning beginners try to find things they can contribute and end up PRing something that maybe isn't that interesting or has no obvious reviewer, or maybe it's just not really a good contribution and would take a long time to look at, and some of these PRs end up going stale for months. I think getting complete silence on your PR is probably worse than a kind "we're not interested in this right now; take a look at this instead" for new contributors. I do see some downsides to the roadmaps but I think there might be a refinement of the approach that helps with this problem.
Personally I'd be for trying it out (not mandatory; probably not even a majority of PRs organised this way) to see what happens, what issues arise, etc
I don't have much opinion, just want to say that if we do try this out, I am look forwarding to making contribution following roadmaps written by experts:smile:

I suspect a large proportion of roadmaps would not be very helpful for beginners looking for things to contribute because a lot of the intended design (in the lead contributor's head) would be hard to write down in a way that's clear enough for beginners without producing actual Lean code to explain what's intended and various parts of what's appropriate generality etc. would only come out of experimentation with actual Lean code (or because the roadmap is about integrating things that have already been implemented in an external repository). Adding small lemmas in an area where the design has been sufficiently implemented in Lean is likely to be more accessible for beginners than something where significant design work is needed as you go along.

For some areas, once enough API is present it may well be possible to produce a roadmap of the form of 50 useful, fairly self-contained results that don't involve design issues themselves. That sort of roadmap might be more accessible to beginners.

With respect to beginners, I was talking about reviewing not writing. I feel like if there is an explicit "we need this and that and probably this way" it is a much easier starting point to review something, as you actually know there is a need for the thing and can wonder if it fits the bill.
If we end up with roadmaps that only people who are already experts can contribute to, I don't think that would be a success

Just found https://github.com/leanprover-community/project-intentions
Was this announced anywhere?
(I know it's much lighter weight than the roadmap proposal)

Announced at #general > Discussion thread for leanprover-community/intentions @ 💬
Originated from #general > public announcements of closed projects?

That serves a different purpose than roadmaps/projects, it's not an invitation for PRs but rather the opposite, a request for other people to not work on something.

Oh right, I see
That's not how I had understood it - my bad
I welcome other people contributing (say) real algebra to Mathlib I'd just like to know about it so we can coordinate
I guess this intentions thing is more for initial development and roadmaps are more for upstreaming, anyway?
Intentions was an attempt to stop AI scooping humans, but AI is not really listening right now

New contributor here.

Good to know there's consideration of doing this (not knowing what to contribute is a real problem), but I'm not so sure if roadmap is a good idea. (How does it compare with just leaving some TODO in the code, and have some sort of system for searching for these TODO?)

What I do now is, since Tau Ceti has the roadmaps, I either let AI work on a part and use my own brain to try my best to understand the result, or pick some file in Tau Ceti and clean it up with a mix of manual and AI. Either way, I pick a topic that I understand reasonably well, so the bottleneck is learning Lean, not learning both Lean and the math.

Since Tau Ceti obviously depends on Mathlib, more often than not, in order to understand some code or design choices, I use the “Go to definition” feature and land in some Mathlib file, and learn a bit more about Mathlib's design.

How would this differ from contributing to “Mathlib with roadmap”? The only difference I can see is, instead of having human maintainers reviewing your code, you have AI reviewing your code. Which is worse (if AI reviewer is as good at human reviewer, it's trivial to make AI code as good as human code), but then they're “cheaper” than human time as well, and for a beginner, it might well be enough to get sufficiently familiar with the ecosystem to (hopefully, I'm not quite there yet) know what/how to contribute.

I can't say I encourage everyone to do this (cleaning up slop code may either be acceptable or unrewarding, depends on the person. At least, it's less bad with AI assistance. One possible factor is that I have some experience architecturing large programs in other programming languages, which is not necessarily the case for most beginners). At least it leads to me learning a lot about Lean and Mathlib's design (including by asking people here why certain things are designed the way they are if I'm not confident with the AI's response. And occasionally contribute some typo fixes to Mathlib).

(Reading Tau Ceti code does not teach one about Mathlib design choices, but reading Mathlib code and asking questions here does. Alternatively, when I want to see how certain thing ought to be designed, I can ask AI to look for precedent of similar feature in Mathlib and read them, which should be more reliable than asking AI for the answer directly.)

This is just a friendly notification that this proposal has not been forgotten by the maintainer team and is under discussion. I encourage all mathlib contributors to (continue) sharing their thoughts in this thread.
